title: Circumcision, the way of Ibrahim
hookLine: five habits of the fitrah, and the one traced to Ibrahim

cards: Five small habits, listed in one sentence. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says five things belong to the fitrah, the natural way people are made.
In paraphrase: circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, trimming the mustache, clipping the nails, and plucking the armpit hair. Four of them are done again and again. The first one is different.
It's done once, and tradition traces it back to a single person: Ibrahim.

teach.b: Khitan means circumcision: for a boy, the removal of the foreskin. The Qur'an doesn't spell it out; the teaching comes through hadith, and through one name.

In another report in Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet says that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, circumcised himself with an adze, and the report says he was eighty years old. An old man, keeping a sign in his own body.
Why does Ibrahim carry so much weight here? The Qur'an tells the Prophet to follow him.
In Pickthall's translation: "Follow the religion of Abraham, as one by nature upright." Upright by nature: close to the idea of fitrah.

So Muslims keep khitan as part of the millah of Ibrahim, the way of Ibrahim, carried on by those who follow him. Then a neighbor. Jews trace circumcision to Abraham too, in the book of Genesis, as a sign of the covenant.

teach.h: A MARK SHARED WITH A NEIGHBOR.
teach.b: Two families of faith, one shared ancestor, and a shared mark.
Then the schools. Muslim scholars differ on how binding it is: some schools count it obligatory, others a strongly emphasized sunnah.
And families choose different times: some on the seventh day, some later in childhood, some with a celebration. Last, respect. This is a custom of the body and of the family.
The way to learn about it is the way anyone would want their own customs learned: listen, ask kindly, and let the people who keep it explain what it means to them.

how: Muslim families circumcise boys as part of the fitrah and the way of Ibrahim; the timing varies by family and culture, from the first days of life to later childhood, sometimes with a family celebration.

games.q: the Prophet names five things of the fitrah. one of them, a report in Bukhari says, goes back to Ibrahim himself. which one?
games.why: circumcision. the report says Ibrahim circumcised himself, in old age, with an adze.

practice: Think of a custom from your own family that marks a child as belonging: a name, a blessing, a first haircut, a photo on the wall. Picture someone asking about it kindly and really listening, and notice how that feels.
Then think of one kind question you could ask about a custom that isn't yours, and how you'd listen to the answer.
